¶
'''twinne<sup>1</sup>†, twinne<sup>2</sup>†.''' A Middle English spelling of ''twin''<sup>1</sup>, ''twin''<sup>2</sup>.

'''twinner''' (twin′ėr), ''n.'' [< ''twin''<sup>1</sup> + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.] One who or that which produces twins. ''Tusser'', January’s Husbandry.

'''twinning<sup>1</sup>''' (twin′ing), ''n.'' [Verbal n. of ''twin''<sup>1</sup>, ''v.''] The process or state of being twinned: said of crystals. See ''twin''<sup>1</sup>, ''n.'', 3.—{{smaller|'''Secondary twinning''', a molecular reversal produced after the formation of the crystal, for example by pressure, as often observed in crystals of pyroxene and the grains of a crystalline limestone. In many cases this may be artificially imitated.}}

'''twinning<sup>2</sup>†''' (twin′ing), ''n.'' [< ME. ''twynnynge''; verbal n. of ''twin''<sup>2</sup>, ''v.''] Separation; parting.
{{smaller block|<poem>The sothe is, the ''twynnynge'' of us tweyne
Wol us disese and crueliche anoye.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, iv. 1303.}}}}

'''twinning-axis''' (twin′ing-ak″sis), ''n.'' See ''twin''<sup>1</sup>, ''n.'', 3.

'''twinning-machine''' (twin′ing-ma-shēn″), ''n.'' A machine for cutting out the teeth of combs: so called because the combs are cut in pairs or twins. {{smaller|It has a cutter consisting of two chisels which act perpendicularly and alternately upon a plate passed beneath them, each cutting one side of two teeth, and severing one of them from the back of the comb to which it does not belong. ''E. H. Knight.''}}

'''twinning-plane''' (twin′ing-plān), ''n.'' See ''twin''<sup>1</sup>, ''n.'', 3.
readings.c1s3:
¶
'''twinning-saw''' (twin′ing-sâ), ''n.'' A saw for cutting the teeth of combs: so called because the teeth for two combs are cut at one operation, the material being bent over in convex form to bring it within range of the instrument. After the sawing, each tooth is cut separately from the back of the opposite comb by means of a plugging-awl. ''E. H. Knight.''

'''twin-pair''' (twin′pãr), ''n.'' A pair of objects altogether similar and equal and without any third.—{{smaller|'''Twin-pair sheet''', in ''geom.'', the surface of a cubic or higher cone which meets the concentric sphere in two distinct closed curves.}}

'''twin-shell''' (twin′shel), ''n.'' One of the pair of symmetrical shells of the dipleuric nassellarians.

'''twinship''' (twin′ship), ''n.'' [< ''twin''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ship''.] The character or relation of being twin.
{{smaller block|The sentence which has gone forth for the severance of the two measures [the Home-rule Bill and the Irish Land Bill] is irresistible, and . . . the ''twinship'' which has been for the time disastrous to the hopes of Ireland exists no longer.
{{right|''Gladstone'', quoted in the Spectator, No. 3035, p. 1133.}}}}

'''twin-spot''' (twin′spot), ''a.'' Having a pair of like spots: as, the ''twin-spot'' carpet, a British moth.

'''twin-stock''' (twin′stok), ''n.'' A beehive containing two colonies. ''Phin'', Dict. Apiculture, p. 73.

'''twinter''' (twin′tėr), ''n.'' [<ME. *''twinter'', *''twiwintre'', < AS. ''twiwintre'' (= MLG. ''twinter''), two winters

'''twire'''<sup>1</sup>† (twīr), ''v. i.'' [Also ''tweer''; = G. dial. (Bav.) ''zwiren'', ''zwieren'', spy, glance; connected with ''zwerch'', etc., cross: see ''queer''<sup>1</sup> and ''thwart''<sup>1</sup>.] '''1.''' To glance shyly or slyly; look askance; make eyes; leer; peer; pry.
readings.c2s2:
A twofold reason. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>You shall pardon me
For a ''twi-reason'' of state.</poem>
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Magnetick Lady, iii. 4.}}}}

'''twirepipe†''' (twīr′pīp), ''n.'' [< ''twire''<sup>1</sup> + ''pipe''<sup>2</sup>.] One who peeps or peers; a peeping Tom.
{{smaller block|<poem>You are . . . a ''twirepipe'',
A Jeffrey John Bo-peep!</poem>
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Monsieur Thomas, iii. 1.}}}}

'''twirk''' (twėrk), ''v. t.'' [Freq. of ''twire''<sup>3</sup>.] To pull or tug; twitch; twirl.
{{smaller block|If shee have her hand on the pette [pit, dimple] in her cheeke, he is ''twyrking'' of his mustachios.
{{right|''Breton'', Praise of Vertuous Ladies, p. 57. (''Davies'', under ''pette''.)}}}}

'''twirk''' (twėrk), ''n.'' [< ''twirk'', ''v.''] A twitch or twirl. ''Jamieson.'' [Scotch.]

'''twirl''' (twėrl), ''v.'' [Early mod. E. ''twyrle''; < ME. *''twirlen'' (?); cf. D. ''dwarlen'' = G. dial. (Swiss) ''zwirlen'', twirl; prob. connected with AS. ''thwiril'', a churn-staff, stirrer, = OHG. ''dwiril'', MHG. ''twirel'', ''twirl'', G. ''quirl'', ''querl'', a twirling-stick, Bav. ''zwirel'', a stirrer. Cf. Icel. ''thvara'', a stick with a scraper at the end for stirring, Gr. τορύνη, a stirrer, L. ''trua'', a stirrer (see ''trowel''); from the verb represented by ''twire''<sup>3</sup>: see ''twire''<sup>3</sup>, and cf. ''twirk''. Cf. also ''tirl''.] '''I.''' ''trans.'' To cause to revolve rapidly; spin; whirl; turn round and round, usually in an idle, purposeless way; twiddle.
{{smaller block|<poem>Leave ''twirling'' of your hat, and hold your head up,
And speak to the lady.</poem>
{{right|''Fletcher'', Rule a Wife, ii. 3.}}}}
{{smaller block|With what ineffable carelessness would he ''twirl'' his gold chain!
{{right|''Lamb'', Old Actors.}}}}

{{smaller block|Se ȝe the ȝonder pore womman how that she is pyned Withe ''twynlenges'' two.
{{right|''Rom. of Cheuelere Assigne'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 27.}}
We may rede and see like thyng in the lyuyng and the condicōns of the bretheren gemellys callid ''twynlynges.''
{{right|''Boke of Tulle of Old Age'' (ed. Caxton, 1481), g<sup>2</sup>. (''Richardson’s Supp.'')}}}}

'''twin-stock''' (twin′stok), ''n.'' A beehive containing two colonies. ''Phin'', Dict. Apiculture, p. 73.

'''twinter''' (twin′tėr), ''n.'' [<ME. *''twinter'', *''twiwintre'', < AS. ''twiwintre'' (= MLG. ''twinter''), two winters old, < ''twi-'', two, + ''winter'', winter.] A beast two winters old. [Prov. Eng. and Scotch.]

'''twire'''<sup>1</sup>† (twīr), ''v. i.'' [Also ''tweer''; = G. dial. (Bav.) ''zwiren'', ''zwieren'', spy, glance; connected with ''zwerch'', etc., cross: see ''queer''<sup>1</sup> and ''thwart''<sup>1</sup>.] '''1.''' To glance shyly or slyly; look askance; make eyes; leer; peer; pry. {{smaller block|{{right|''B. Jonson'', Sad Shepherd, ii. 1.}}
I saw the wench that ''twired'' and twinkled at thee.
{{right|''Fletcher'', Women Pleased, iv. 1.}}
The ''tweering'' constable of Finsbury, with his bench of brown-bill men. {{right|''Middleton'', Father Hubbard’s Tales.}}
If I was rich, I could ''twire'' and loll as well as the best of them. {{right|''Steele'', Conscious Lovers, i. 1.}}}}
'''2.''' To twinkle; sparkle; wink.
{{smaller block|When sparkling stars ''twire'' not, thou gild’st the even.
{{right|''Shak.'', Sonnets, xxviii.}}
<poem>The sun, . . .
Who with a fervent eye looks through the ''twyring'' glades,
And his dispersed rays commixeth with the shades.</poem>
{{right|''Drayton'', Polyolbion, xiii. 169.}}}}

'''twire<sup>1</sup>†''' (twīr), ''n.'' [Also ''tweer''; < ''twire''<sup>1</sup>, ''v.''] A sly glance; a leer.
{{smaller block|<poem>The formal Bows,
The affected smiles, the silly By-words, and Amorous
''Tweers'' in passing.</poem>
{{right|''Etherege'', Man of Mode, iii. 3.}}}}

'''twire<sup>2</sup>†''' (twīr), ''n.'' [= D. ''tweern'' = MHG. ''zwirn'', ''zwirm'', G. ''zwirn'', twine; akin to ''twine''<sup>1</sup>.] A twisted filament; a thread.
{{smaller block|They put the cocons in hot water, and so stirring them about with a kind of rod, the ends of the silk ''twires'' of the cocons stick to it, which they laying on upon a turning reel draw off from the cocons. {{right|''Locke'', Obs. upon Silk.}}}}

'''twire<sup>3</sup>''' (twīr), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''twired'', ppr. ''twiring''. [Perhaps a dial. form of *''twere'', < ME. *''thweren'', < AS. *''thweran'', in comp. ''ā-thweran'', agitate, stir, = OHG. ''dweran'', MHG. ''twern'', G. dial. (Bav.) ''zweren'', stir. Cf. ''twirk'', ''twirl''.] To twist; twirl.
{{smaller block|No sooner doth a yong man see his sweet-heart coming, but he . . . ''twires'' his beard.
{{right|''Burton'', Anat. of Mel., p. 534.}}}}

'''twireason†''' (twī′rē″zn), ''n.'' [< ''twi-'' + ''reason''.] A twofold reason. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>You shall pardon me
For a ''twi-reason'' of state.</poem>
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Magnetick Lady, iii. 4.}}}}

'''twirepipe†''' (twīr′pīp), ''n.'' [< ''twire''<sup>1</sup> + ''pipe''<sup>2</sup>.] One who peeps or peers; a peeping Tom.
{{smaller block|<poem>You are . . . a ''twirepipe'',
A Jeffrey John Bo-peep!</poem>
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Monsieur Thomas, iii. 1.}}}}

'''twirk''' (twėrk), ''v. t.'' [Freq. of ''twire''<sup>3</sup>.] To pull or tug; twitch; twirl.
{{smaller block|If shee have her hand on the pette [pit, dimple] in her cheeke, he is ''twyrking'' of his mustachios.
{{right|''Breton'', Praise of Vertuous Ladies, p. 57. (''Davies'', under ''pette''.)}}}}

'''twirk''' (twėrk), ''n.'' [< ''twirk'', ''v.''] A twitch or twirl. ''Jamieson.'' [Scotch.]

'''twirl''' (twėrl), ''v.'' [Early mod. E. ''twyrle''; < ME. *''twirlen'' (?); cf. D. ''dwarlen'' = G. dial. (Swiss) ''zwirlen'', twirl; prob. connected with AS. ''thwiril'', a churn-staff, stirrer, = OHG. ''dwiril'', MHG. ''twirel'', ''twirl'', G. ''quirl'', ''querl'', a twirling-stick, Bav. ''zwirel'', a stirrer. Cf. Icel. ''thvara'', a stick with a scraper at the end for stirring, Gr. τορύνη, a stirrer, L. ''trua'', a stirrer (see ''trowel''); from the verb represented by ''twire''<sup>3</sup>: see ''twire''<sup>3</sup>, and cf. ''twirk''. Cf. also ''tirl''.] '''I.''' ''trans.'' To cause to revolve rapidly; spin; whirl; turn round and round, usually in an idle, purposeless way; twiddle.
{{smaller block|<poem>Leave ''twirling'' of your hat, and hold your head up,
And speak to the lady.</poem>
{{right|''Fletcher'', Rule a Wife, ii. 3.}}}}
{{smaller block|With what ineffable carelessness would he ''twirl'' his gold chain!
{{right|''Lamb'', Old Actors.}}}}

'''To twirl one’s thumbs''', to twiddle the thumbs, for lack of better employment; hence, to do nothing; be idle.

{{smaller block|Upon my word, Walter, you are pretty cool! Will it amuse me, pray, to ''twirl my thumbs'' in your studio?
{{right|''W. E. Norris'', Miss Shafto, xxiv.}}}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To move round; especially, to revolve rapidly; be whirled about.

{{smaller block|Take bothe your handes, and ''twyrle'' vpon his [a sheep’s] eye, and if he be ruddy, and haue reed stryndes in the white of the eye, than he is sounde.
{{right|''Fitzherbert'', Husbandry (Eng. Dialect Soc.), p. 51.}}
I had arrived at very considerable agility in the waltzing line, and could ''twirl'' round the room with him at such a pace as made the old gentleman pant again.
{{right|''Thackeray'', Fitz-Boodle’s Confessions, Dorothea.}}
Away they jumped, with more and more vigour, till Maggie’s hair flew from behind her ears, and ''twirled'' about like an animated mop. ''George Eliot'', Mill on the Floss, ii. 1.}}

'''2.''' To twine; wind; coil; curl. [Rare.]

<poem>So when the wriggling snake is snatch’d on high
In eagle’s claws, and hisses in the sky,
Around the foe his ''twirling'' tail he flings,
And twists her legs, and writhes about her wings.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Addison'', tr. of Ovid’s Metamorph., iv.}}}}

'''twirl''' (twėrl), ''n.'' [< ''twirl'', ''v.''] '''1.''' A rapid circular motion.

{{smaller block|He watched the wreaths of steam, until, at the special instant of projection, he caught up the iron vessel and gave it one delicate ''twirl'', causing it to send forth one gentle hiss.
{{right|''Dickens'', Our Mutual Friend, i. 13.}}}}

{{smaller block|Jem, in all the pride of newly-acquired penmanship, used to dazzle her eyes by extraordinary graces and ''twirls.''
{{right|''Mrs. Gaskell'', Mary Barton, xxi.}}}}

'''twirler''' (twėr′lėr), ''n.'' [< ''twirl'' + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.] One who or that which twirls.
{{smaller block|Critics [in base-ball] are still looking for the pitcher par excellence. Although they acknowledge that the point of excellence has been nearly approached at times, still their ideal ''twirler'' of the diminutive globe has not yet made his appearance.
{{right|''Tribune Book of Sports'', p. 81.}}}}

'''twissel†''' (twis′l), ''a.'' and ''n.'' [Also ''twistle;'' < ME. ''twisel, twisil'' (= MHG. ''zwisel''), < AS. ''twi-'', etc., two: see ''twi-'', ''two'', and cf. ''twist'', etc.] '''I.''' ''a.'' Double; twofold.
{{smaller block|Enhancing, and pride, and the shreude wei, and the mouth of the ''twisil'' tunge I wlate [loathe].
{{right|''Wyclif'', Prov. viii. 13.}}}}

'''II.''' ''n.'' '''1.''' That which is double, as a double fruit, or fruit growing in pairs.
{{smaller block|<poem>As from a tree we sundrie times espie
A ''twissell'' grow by Natures subtile might,
And beeing two, for cause they grow so nie,
For one are tane, and so appeare in sight.</poem>
{{right|''Turberville'', The Lover Wisheth, etc.}}}}

'''2.''' That part of a tree where the branches separate from the trunk or bole.

'''twissel-tongued†''' (twis′l-tungd), ''a.'' [ME. ''twisiltunged;'' < ''twissel'' + ''tongue'' + ''-ed''<sup>2</sup>.] Double-tongued. {{smaller block|Repref forsothe and strif the euel man shal eritagen, and eche synnere enuyous and ''twisil-tungid''.
{{right|''Wyclif'', Ecclus. vi. 1.}}}}

'''twist''' (twist), ''n.'' [< ME. ''twist'', < AS. ''twist'' (in comp. ''mæst-twist''), a rope, = MD. ''twist'', a forked branch, = Icel. ''tvistr'', the two or deuce in cards; also in another sense, = D. ''twist'' = LG. ''twist'' = MHG. G. ''zwist'' = Sw. Dan. ''tvist'', discord, strife, odds, = Icel. ''tvist'', in the phrase ''ā tvist og bast'', scattered to the four winds; with formative ''-st'', < AS. ''twi-'', etc., two: see ''twi-''. Cf. ''twine''<sup>1</sup>, ''twin''<sup>1</sup>.] '''1.''' A thread, cord, rope, or the like made of two or more strands wound one about another; anything resembling such a rope or coil.
{{smaller block|<poem>Breaking his oath and resolution like
A ''twist'' of rotten silk. ''Shak.'', Cor., v. 6. 96.</poem>
<poem>I saw about her spotlesse wrist
Of blackest silk a curious ''twist''.</poem>
{{right|''Herrick'', Upon a Black ''Twist'' Rounding the Arm of the [Countess of Carlisle.}}
<poem>A ''twist'' of gold was round her hair.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Merlin and Vivien.}}}}
{{smaller block|Specifically — (''a'') A kind of strong, close silk thread used for sewing.

All the fine sewing silk was proved to be free from lead or other metal. But we found metal very abundant in what is called “tailors’ ''twist''” and “hatters’ ''twist'',” especially the latter. {{right|''Ure'', Dict., IV. 524.}}
(''b'') A kind of cotton yarn of several varieties.

Being from two roves in place of one, it [cotton yarn for stockings] is called double-spun ''twist''.
{{right|''Encyc. Brit.'', VI. 500.}}
(''c'') In ''weaving'', the warp-thread of the web. ''E. H. Knight.''
(''d'') A loaf or roll of twisted dough baked.}}

{{smaller block|In short order the dough is turned into ''twists'', high loaves, pan loaves, and other styles of the same quality.
{{right|''Sci. Amer.'', N. S., LIX. 273.}}}}
{{smaller|(''e'') A kind of manufactured tobacco made in the form of a rope or thick cord.}}

'''2†.''' A fabric made with a double and hence heavy thread; coarse cloth. Compare ''twine''<sup>1</sup>, ''n.'', 1, and ''twine''<sup>1</sup>, ''a.''
{{smaller block|<poem>Ne to weare garments base of wollen ''twist'',
But with the finest silkes us to aray.</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', Mother Hub. Tale, l. 460.}}}}

'''3†.''' A forked branch; a twig; a spray.
{{smaller block|<poem>On his bak she stood,
And caughte hire by a ''twiste'', and up she gooth.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Merchant’s Tale, l. 1105.}}
So long as a sprigge, ''twist'', or braunche is yong, it is flexible and bowable to any thing a man can desire.
{{right|''Stubbes'', Anat. of Abuses (ed. Furnivall), I. 76.}}}}

'''4†.''' Same as ''fork'', 5.
{{smaller block|A man of common heigth might easilie go vnder his ''twist'' without stooping, a stature incredible.
{{right|''Harrison'', Descrip. of Britain, v. (Holinshed’s Chron., I.).}}}}

'''5†.''' A hinge.
{{smaller block|And the herris, ether ''twistis'', of the temple schulen greetli sowne. {{right|''Wyclif'', Amos viii. 3.}}}}

'''6.''' An intertwining or interlacing; a knot or net, or other interwoven contrivance.
{{smaller block|<poem>He tames a Heifer, and on either side,
On either horn a three-fold ''twist'' he ty’d
Of Osiar twigs.</poem>
{{right|''Sylvester'', tr. of Du Bartas’s Weeks, ii., The Handy-Crafts.}}}}

'''7.''' A spiral form, disposition, or arrangement, such as may be produced by bending round both ends of an object in opposite directions; also, spiral or progressive rotary motion, or the path<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
